title: Seeing the ox
hookLine: third picture: he glimpses the ox itself

lines: A BIRD SINGS. THE WILLOWS ARE GREEN.
cards: A bird sings somewhere in the branches. The sun is warm, the wind is soft, the willows along the bank are green. That's the verse for the third oxherding picture, and it's oddly ordinary.
No thunder, no vision in the clouds. The herdsman has followed prints for a long time, reading about the ox, talking about the ox.
Then, on a pleasant afternoon, he hears that bird, looks up, and there among the willows is the ox itself.

teach.b: First, from evidence to contact. The preface says, in paraphrase, that he finds the way in through sound: hearing clearly opens the gate.
Reading about honey and tasting it are different kinds of knowing, and this is the move from one to the other.

teach.h: THE GLIMPSE COMES THROUGH THE SENSES.
teach.b: Second, the glimpse comes through the senses, not around them. The verse keeps him right where he is: birdsong, sunlight, wind, willows.
Some Zen teachers say the way isn't hidden behind daily life; it's shining through it. The verse even asks where the ox could possibly hide.
Third, seen, but not yet caught. In some well-known drawings only part of the ox shows, its head or its hindquarters, the rest behind a tree. A glimpse can be completely real and still be brief.
Fourth, now he knows for himself. Without a glimpse, all the tracks in the world stay secondhand.
In ordinary life it can be very small: a moment where the mind is clear and nothing is missing, the sound of rain heard all the way through. It may pass in seconds.
The third picture says that's enough to change the search, because the old question, is there even an ox, has been answered.

how: In Zen communities the third oxherding picture is often read as a first direct glimpse of one's own nature, and teachers use it to remind students that such a glimpse is real but is the start of training, not the end.

o: a vision in the clouds that ends the search for good
reading enough about the way to describe it well
a real glimpse of the way through the senses, not yet held

games.q: seeing the ox: tap the pairs.
p: the ordinary scene of the glimpse
part of the ox behind a tree

s: in the third picture the herdsman has caught the ox
he only glimpses it; catching comes in the fourth picture.
the verse sets the glimpse in an ordinary scene
birdsong, warm sun, soft wind, green willows.
a glimpse that passes quickly doesn't count
the picture treats the glimpse as real: now he knows for himself the ox is there.

games.q: you're the herdsman, following prints. a bird sings, you look up, and part of the ox shows behind a tree. what has just happened?
o: you've seen the ox for yourself, but not caught it.
games.why: the third picture is a real glimpse of the ox itself, not secondhand evidence. catching it is still ahead, and tomorrow it fights the rope.

practice: Let your eyes rest, and instead of looking for anything, let sound come to you, the way the bird's song came to the herdsman: the hum of a fridge, a car outside, your own breath.
Hear one sound all the way through, from its start to its fading. If a moment comes that is simply clear, notice it without grabbing; if none comes, listening is still the practice.

wordCard.voice: Seeing the ox. The third oxherding picture: through birdsong and sunlight, the herdsman glimpses the ox itself, real, but not yet caught. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (jianniu): 'seeing the ox', the name of the third oxherding picture.

carryVoice: Your line: there it is. A glimpse can be brief and still be completely real. Twelve twenty-three days in.
